items.content:
RT @IAMERICAbooted: A common misconception is that frontier models only trained on the internet.  This is false.  They all bought books, scanned them, then destroyed them.

People confuse harness and context activity with models.  The reason you see reddit a lot in the search results of LLMs is not because it's retrieving that information feom the model.  It's doing a websearch in real time with a tool that has nothing to do with the model.  

Models are trained on point-in-time information.  The reason websearch is so valuable is because information in models is stale.  The agents use websearch with the model and other context to produce better output.

Reasoning can be broken down into instructions that tell the model to recurse until a specified sentinel is hit.  It's essentially loops of instructions to models that are updated in real time.  LLM produces output from the query, a loop feeds it back in.  It's an algorithm under the hood.

items.content:
RT @antoniosarosi: Taking over someone else's unfinished work in 2022:

Open GitHub, there's a PR there.
+673 -241 diff.

Checkout the branch, run tests.
They pass.

Spend 2 hours reading the code to understand it.

There's a weird if statement that you don't understand why it's there.
You ask the coworker who opened the PR.

He says it's because some obscure payload field can be null and now it all makes sense, you understand all the code.

Read the ticket again to see what's missing and write rest of code.

+871 -308 final diff.
Merge PR.

✅ Done.

Taking over someone else's work in 2026:

Open GitHub. There's a PR there.
+87341 -32651 diff.

Tell Claude to read the ticket and see what's left.
Claude comes up with 5 bullet points of what's left to do. You understand none of them.

There are 15 markdown files in the PR your coworker's agent dumped for future context.
You open them. 3000 lines each. You understand none of it.

Ask Claude to explain it like you're 5.
Claude outputs words that are coherent but you still understand none of it.

You tell Claude to make diagrams to explain the architecture.
A tiny bit of it starts making sense.

There's some weird service "Transactional Reconciliation Service" you don't understand why it's there. Claude says it shouldn't be there and the markdown files don't specify why it's there.

You ask the coworker about that service.
He has no idea what you're talking about, he needs to ask his agent.

His Claude makes an artifact that explains why that service is slop that was written by the subagent who implemented it and shouldn't be there at all.

The coworker hands that artifact to you. He hasn't read it.

You hand the artifact to your Claude. Your Claude advices to remove the service and proposes 4 different solutions to replace it.

You understand none of the solutions but there is one which seems to make more sense. You ask the coworker if that's a good call.

He has no idea what any of that means, he asks his agent. His agent says it's a good solution but it's missing an important edge case. He copy pastes the agent output in Slack.

You copy paste the Slack message into your Claude. Your Claude says that you're absolutely right, that this is an important edge case that was not handled in the initial solution. Claude proposes a small fix to cover it and asks if it should implement it along with the other 5 bullet points.

You say ok, Claude starts writing code. PR diff grows to +97564 -41698.

You ask Claude if everything in the ticket is implemented. Claude starts reviewing the code.

Claude says that most of it is implemented, but comes up with 5 bullet points of things that are missing.

You are confused, it already came up with 5 bullet points the first time you asked. These seem different bullet points that only came up after reviewing the code though, so you say ok, implement it.

Claude writes code.
PR +102467 -45790 diff.

You ask if now it's all done.
Claude reviews the code. Says it's mostly done but there 3 low priority items that are not yet implemented.

You don't understand any of the items but since they're low priority you figure out they don't matter much, so you click merge.

PR spends 3 hours in the merge queue for CI to go green, then it merges.

Next Monday your coworker asks his agent to deploy to AWS.
Your agent's code now runs in production.

2 hours later the whole backend is down. No one knows why.

Your coworker asks his agent to investigate. After 20 minutes it finds the code that threw an unhandled error when some payload came up with an obscure null field.

Your coworker doesn't recognize any of that code and his agent says it should not be there but you wrote it so your coworker should check with you first.

He asks you about that code.

You've never seen that code in your entire life.
You ask your agent about it.

Your Claude says the error was thrown because the code never expected that obscure field to be null.

The code was in "Transactional Reconciliation Service".

items.content:
RT @oegerikus: Last week, a critical vulnerability in Java was made public.

It's called Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938). Researchers at Calif report that an attacker can send deliberately broken text to a server running tools like Jira, Confluence or Jenkins, and take it over without a password.

@fede_k and @hkashfi at @Xbow recreated the bug in our lab to see what it can do. Here are 5 things you should know:

- Researchers found the bug in one hour and had a working attack two hours later. Time to exploit is shrinking fast.

- In our lab, a test server returned about 5x the data it should have, including a secret marker only the server knew.

- Don't wait for a confirmed attack before you patch. Even a rumor of a flaw like this is reason enough to act.

- It only affects certain Intel and AMD chips that support AVX-512. ARM chips are unaffected.

- A fixed version of Java came out on November 17, and there's a temporary workaround if you can't update right away.

See which chips and cloud machines could be at risk with our Security Lab's searchable matrix. It covers CPU models and the machines offered by AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and seven other cloud providers.

Read the full field notes here:

https://t.co/vCZiNUNbQ0

items.content:
RT @DesmondShum: The Shadow Network Behind China’s AI Chip Workaround

Follow the money through Southeast Asia’s data centres and you find private equity financiers, Wall Street banks, Beijing-backed lenders and the family firm of the US commerce secretary.

@ChrisRMcGuire @RyanFedasiuk 

I highly recommend reading the writeup in the following post in full. It follows the money behind Southeast Asia’s AI data centres, from the investors who put up the equity and the banks that lent against the contracts to the Chinese tech giants renting the computing power.

Two things stood out to me.

First, look at who put these deals together. Bain backed Bridge. Partners Group backed Digital Halo. Coatue and Hillhouse led DayOne’s $4.5 billion round, joined by Taiwan’s Achi Capital. ByteDance also borrowed directly. Citi and JPMorgan arranged its $29.6 billion corporate loan, and 15 Chinese banks reportedly committed $18.9 billion of it. The Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, or known as Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative bank, is also a financier in these efforts.

The bet was simple. Keep the Nvidia chips offshore and rent the computing power to Chinese companies that would need a US licence to buy those same chips. 

Secondly, it’s about Luknik and Nvidia’s first SE Asia cloud partner. Bitdeer, a Singapore-based bitcoin miner, became one of Nvidia’s early cloud partners in Southeast Asia in March 2024. Two months later, while Howard Lutnick still ran Cantor Fitzgerald, a traditional bond trading firm, suddenly became involved in equity financing, helped place Tether’s $100 million investment in Bitdeer.

By 2026, Lutnick was commerce secretary and his sons ran Cantor, a sales agent for Bitdeer’s share offering of up to $1 billion. According to The New York Times, Lutnick pushed for a weaker chip rule that would have benefited Bitdeer’s Malaysian AI centre. Its likely customer? Tencent.

What ethics advice, if any, did Lutnick seek before weighing in on a rule that could benefit a client of his family’s firm?

items.content:
RT @superalesha: I deleted Linux completely, baked Qwen3-0.6B into a 24 KB pure x86-64 assembly OS, and it runs up to 54% faster than native Linux llama.cpp.

The entire Multiboot OS binary (asm-llm-os.elf) is 24,252 bytes, written from scratch without Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. It boots in 74 to 94 ms straight into 64-bit Long Mode, wakes every CPU core over APIC, maps the 614 MiB Q8_0 weights directly from physical RAM, and drops you into a live multi-turn KV-cache chat over VGA, PS/2 keyboard, and serial.

I ran head-to-head CPU benchmarks against llama.cpp (Q8_0, -ngl 0) on the same AMD EPYC 7642:

- 1 thread hits 23.67 tok/s vs 16.63 (+42%)
- 4 threads hit 78.89 tok/s vs 51.08 (+54%)
- 8 threads hit 118.08 tok/s vs 80.79 (+46%)
- 16 threads hit 134.94 tok/s vs 103.03 (+31%, 136.6 peak)

On a diskless 0 GB Proxmox VM (2014 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 2 GiB RAM), it boots straight to the prompt in under 5 seconds (95 ms kernel boot) and runs live out of RAM at 78 tok/s decode and up to 111.5 tok/s prefill, with a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO builder included too. Output stays bit-exact across thread counts and matches all 64 greedy tokens against PyTorch FP32 (0.99965 cosine).

The 14.7 KB Linux ELF build (FAST_Q8=1 INT8xINT8 AVX2+F16C) also beats llama.cpp by 18% to 36% from 1 to 40 threads, and booting bare metal with 2 MiB huge pages squeezes out another 10% on top.

Repo, ISO builder, and Proxmox setup guide are in the reply below.

items.content:
RT @nextronresearch: Our THOR Thunderstorm-based artifact scanning pipeline spotted a new npm package clamp4js@1.0.13 related to the "Enterotoxin" campaign that @safedepio and @ossmalware reported on two days ago.

Like those packages, it poses as a tiny clamp() helper. The siblings copy the popular clamp package, which has roughly 500k weekly downloads. The harmful code runs at install time, so a single npm install on a developer laptop or CI runner is enough to trigger it.

What's new compared with clampony 1.0.11:

The payload URLs are now hidden. The readable officeapps/google URLs are decoys, and a mod-257 substitution (install.js:29-48) decodes them into the known Pastebin and calcal[.]ru links
Stage 2 is now saved to %TEMP%, and the install sends a beacon to urlto[.]me
It still does not run stage 2. The operator is one step away from execution.

Stage 2 is unchanged (same SHA256 as already reported). It is a Windows-only stealer that:

- collects SSH keys, AWS/GCP/Azure/kube/docker/terraform credentials, .npmrc/.pypirc/.git-credentials, FileZilla/WinSCP/MobaXterm configs, shell histories and Telegram sessions
- zips them into sysvolume[.]zip and sends the archive to a Telegram bot
- installs the Enterotoxin RAT, which runs Python and batch tasks sent by the operator, logs keystrokes and persists as a fake Microsoft Store updater

IOCs: https://t.co/evCVRHAoXi

RT @TheDFIRReport: 🔍 Inside a threat actor's open directory: automated, full-chain attacks on fintech

While reviewing an exposed open directory, we recovered the operator's own engagement logs produced by an agentic offensive framework ("ARTEX") running a templated "full-chain" playbook across dozens of fintech, crypto-payment, and iGaming targets.

The directory held 46 documented findings, each with reproduction steps and, in many cases, exfiltrated secrets:
🔴 11 Critical · 🟠 13 High · 🟡 16 Medium · 🟢 6 Low

Recurring tradecraft:
• Cloud credentials (API keys, DB passwords) harvested from publicly exposed database dumps and backup files
• Path traversal escalated to production DB credentials and root SSH private keys — full host + lateral compromise
• Redis reached via Gopher SSRF, then abused for remote code execution
• Secrets lifted straight from front-end JS bundles (Vite/Angular/Ember): access passwords, 2FA seeds, live payment keys
• IDOR / broken object-level authorization exposing customer PII at scale
• Exposed observability & docs: Spring Boot Actuator, Prometheus /metrics, public Swagger

#DFIR #ThreatIntel #CTI #InfoSec

items.content:
RT @AdamCohen8: Story time about how ‘Extreme Ownership’ by @jockowillink and @LeifBabin changed me. 

I was in basic cadet training (BCT) at the US Air Force Academy as a 17-year-old. 

About two weeks in, one of our flight cadre (cadet version of military training instructor) started yelling at me to cup my hands. I was pretty sure I was cupping my hands correctly so I didn’t know what to do. 

I came into basic having marched competitively at a very high level through Civil Air Patrol and jROTC. This made me confident that I wasn’t doing anything wrong. 

Finally I just opened my hands and put them back the way I was doing it before. He replied “thank you” so that seemed to confirm that he just wanted to yell at me for something. 

Then I got covid (this was in 2020) and was isolated from my flight for a week. While in isolation, they allowed us to sit in the bleachers to watch our flights march in a ceremony. 

During the ceremony I got to see the cadre that was correcting me march for the first time. Before this, I was always in the formation and couldn’t see him. 

His marching was objectively terrible. He was swinging his arms way too far forward and not bringing them back past the front of his thigh. 

This confirmed to me that he had no idea what he was talking about and must have been yelling at me for the sake of yelling. 

I returned to my flight after a week and continued the cycle of getting yelled at to cup my hands and repeating my solution from earlier. 

One day, I guess he caught on that I wasn’t changing anything and he erupted at me. As he was berating me, he accidentally spit on my face and I recoiled. This pissed him off further and he sent me up the chain for what the military calls a “verbal counseling.”

In the verbal counseling, I met a MSgt that I am eternally grateful to. He let me tell the story you just read without interrupting. 

Then he replied, “why did you never tell him that you didn’t understand his critiques?” 

I said that I thought he was just looking for something to yell at me for. Other than this I was performing very well. I realized as I was saying it, that if that was the case, it wouldn’t have escalated to this. 

I realized that even though I was objectively correct in terms of the marching and he was mistaken in his corrections, I could have handled the situation better. 

The MSgt asked me if I had ever read Extreme Ownership. I said that I had heard of it but never read it. He spent some time summarizing the lessons of the book and I wanted to know more. 

Basic during Covid meant we had to sit through a lot of briefings on Teams via our laptops from our dorm rooms. 

While I was supposed to be listening to briefings, I found a way to read the book on my computer. That night, the cadre forgot to take our laptops away from us and I stayed up till 2 AM to finish the book. 

It completely changed the way I view leadership. Now, whenever something goes wrong, I do my best to only think about what I could have done differently to cause a different outcome. 

I worked basic as flight cadre going into my junior and senior years. Both times, I kept a copy of the book on me and read several passages to my flight. 

This experience also made me a better cadre. Most people think that the job is just about yelling at people and being scary. It’s not. It’s about training them to transition from being a civilian to a member of the military. 

I kept my intensity at a 10 the whole time and never let an infraction slide, but I never made up a reason to yell. 

If you yell all the time, your yelling becomes meaningless. But if you reserve yelling for when it is absolutely necessary to convey the seriousness of the matter, it carries so much more weight. 

Anyways, thanks for listening to my TED talk. Happy Thanksgiving!
